## This week's learning objectives

When we don't have access to the population we want to compare our sample to, how can we run a statistical analysis?

- We rephrase our problem into a comparison between our sample and a specific hypothesised value.
- Our null distribution becomes a t-distribution (which has slightly fatter tails, essentially meaning that we assign slightly greater probability to more extreme values).
- The t-distribution looks more and more like a normal distribution, the bigger our sample is (and thus the more "degrees of freedom" the distribution has).

What kind of statistical test lets us compare our sample to a specific hypothesised value?

- A one-sample t-test.



# What do we do when we don't have access to the population?

## What do we do when we don't have access to the population?

::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="45%"}

**Last week, we knew the population we wanted to compare our sample to:**

<br>

```{r echo=F, fig.width=5, fig.height=3, fig.align = 'center'}

mu <- 100
sigma <- 15

x <- seq((mu - 4*sigma), (mu + 4*sigma), length.out = 1000)
y <- dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

p_iq_pop <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "#0F4C81") +
  labs(x = "IQ scores in the population", y = "Density") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(
    (mu - 4*sigma), (mu + 4*sigma), by = sigma)
    ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = 'Source Sans 3', size = 24),
    axis.title = ggplot2::element_text(color = dapr1blue)
  ) +
  NULL

p_iq_pop
```

:::
:::{.column width="10%"}
:::
:::{.column width="45%"}

**In real life, we'll basically never know the population that we want to compare any of our samples to.**

<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>

:::hcenter
**???**
:::

:::
::::


::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="45%"}

- Our RQ asked whether bilingual adults had a higher IQ than the general population.
- We knew that in the population, IQ is normally distributed with mean of 100 and standard deviation of 15.
- This let us come up with the null distribution—what sample means **would** look like **if** H0 were true—based on properties of the population.

:::
:::{.column width="10%"}
:::
:::{.column width="45%"}

- Real life is basically always like this: we don't know the true population mean or how variable the population is.
- So we can't use the population to figure out our null distribution.
- **So how do we know what to compare our sample to?**

:::
::::


## The answer: The t-distribution

```{r echo=F, fig.width=8, fig.height=2.5}
#| out.width: 1000px

x <- seq(-6, 6, length.out = 1000)
y <- dt(x, df = 2)
z <- dnorm(x)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y, z = z)

p_t <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "seagreen4") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(
    x = x,
    ymin = 0,
    ymax = y
  ), 
  fill = 'seagreen4',
  alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "t", y = "Density") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = 'Source Sans 3', size = 24),
    axis.title = ggplot2::element_text(color = dapr1blue)
  ) +
  NULL

p_t
```

It looks a lot like a normal distribution (overlaid in blue), but it's less pointy in the middle and fatter at the tails.

```{r echo=F, fig.width=8, fig.height=2.5}
#| out.width: 1000px
p_t +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(x = x, ymin = 0, ymax = z),
    alpha = 0.4,
    fill = dapr1blue
  ) +
  annotate(geom = 'text', y = 0.3, x = 4, label = 'normal distribution\nwith mean 0, SD 1',
           colour = dapr1blue,
           family = 'Source Sans 3',
           size = 8) +
   geom_curve(x=1.5, xend=0.2, y=0.37, yend=0.38, col=dapr1blue, curvature = 0.2, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.1, "npc")), linewidth = 1.5) +
  xlab(NULL) +
  NULL
```

The fat tails put more probability on extreme values, so that we don't rule them out as much, since after all we don't know what the population might look like.

## The t-distribution has different shapes

All of these are t-distributions with different **degrees of freedom (df):**

```{r echo=F, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5}
tibble(x = c(-5, 5)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, args = list(df = 2), colour = '#85DB8F', linewidth = 2) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, args = list(df = 5), colour = '#5DB367', linewidth = 2) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, args = list(df = 99), colour = '#528B59', linewidth = 2) +
  labs(x = 't', y = 'Density') +
  annotate(geom = 'text', x = 3, y = 0.38, label = 'df = 2 ', colour = '#85DB8F', size = 9, family = 'Source Sans 3', hjust = 0) +
  annotate(geom = 'text', x = 3, y = 0.35, label = 'df = 5 ', colour = '#5DB367', size = 9, family = 'Source Sans 3', hjust = 0) +
  annotate(geom = 'text', x = 3, y = 0.32, label = 'df = 99', colour = '#528B59', size = 9, family = 'Source Sans 3', hjust = 0) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  NULL
```

You don't need to know exactly what df is.
Just know that **it's closely related related to sample size:**

- if we have a sample size $n$ of 100, 
- then we have 99 degrees of freedom.
- **For tests involving t-distributions, the df is always $n - 1$.**

So our sample size determines the shape of the t-distribution that we will use as our null distribution.

Why does it work this way?
Because the more data we have, the better a guess we can make about the population.


# Let's see how the t-test works

## Let's see how the t-test works

<br>

Recall from last week the five steps of NHST:

1. Based on your RQ, define the null and alternative hypotheses.
2. Collect sample data and determine the appropriate null distribution.
3. Calculate the test statistic for our observed sample.
4. Make a decision about whether or not to reject H0.
5. Interpret this decision in the context of the RQ.

<br>

We'll go through them one by one as we walk through the logic of a **one-sample t-test.**


# Step 1: Based on RQ, define H0 and H1

## Activity: Match RQs to the appropriate H1

<br>

https://app.wooclap.com/events/SKTAABC/

## Our RQ this week

<br>

**RQ: In healthy adults, is average body temperature different from the standard reference value of 37C?**

<br>

**The null hypothesis (H0)** is always that any difference or effect we're interested in **does not exist.**

- So our H0 here is that average body temperature $\mu$ is equal to 37C.


::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- In fancy math notation:

$$
H_0 : \mu = 37
$$
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
- In plain text:

:::{style="font-size:180%;"}
```
H0: mu = 37
```
:::

:::
::::

<br>

**The alternative hypothesis (H1)** is that the difference or effect we're interested in **does exist.**

- So our H1 here is that average body temperature is *not* equal to 37C.



::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- In fancy math notation:

$$
H_1 : \mu \neq 37
$$
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
- In plain text:

:::{style="font-size:180%;"}
```
H0: mu != 37
```
:::

:::
::::



# Step 2: Gather data and <br> determine the appropriate <br> null distribution

## This week's data: Body temperatures

<br>

```{r message=F}
temp_sample <- read_csv('https://uoepsy.github.io/data/BodyTemperatures.csv')
```

<br>

```{r message=F}
glimpse(temp_sample)
```

<br>

```{r fig.width = 12, fig.height = 4}
#| out.width: 1200px
#| code-fold: true
temp_sample |>
  ggplot(aes(x = BodyTemp)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 0, fill = '#0F4C81')
```

**Our key question: How likely would it be to get a sample like this one, if H0 were true? (That is, if body temps were truly 37C on average?)**


## If H0 were true, what would we expect to see?

If H0 is true—if body temperatures in reality do have a mean of 37C—then:

- The difference between our sample mean and the value 37 should be pretty small, close to zero.
- But the sampling process is random, so we would also expect to observe some differences that are off to either side of zero.

How much variability around zero should we expect, exactly, if the H0 is true?

<br>

**The answer to that question is the t-distribution:**

<br>

```{r echo=F, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
#| out.width: 1000px

x <- seq(-6, 6, length.out = 1000)
y <- dt(x, df = 49)
z <- dnorm(x)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y, z = z)

p_t49 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "seagreen4") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(
    x = x,
    ymin = 0,
    ymax = y
  ), 
  fill = 'seagreen4',
  alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "t", y = "Density") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = 'Source Sans 3', size = 24),
    axis.title = ggplot2::element_text(color = dapr1blue)
  ) +
  NULL

p_t49 +
  annotate(geom = 'text', x = 2.1, y = 0.2, label = 'df = (n minus 1) = 49 ', colour = 'seagreen4', size = 9, family = 'Source Sans 3', hjust = 0) +
  NULL
```


## So do we expect differences of $\pm$ 2-ish °C?

<br>

```{r echo=F, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
#| out.width: 1000px
p_t49 +
  annotate(geom = 'text', x = 2.1, y = 0.2, label = 'df = (n minus 1) = 49 ', colour = 'seagreen4', size = 9, family = 'Source Sans 3', hjust = 0) +
  NULL
```

No—if H0 were true, we would expect differences of $\pm$ 2-ish **t-values.**

- A t-value tells you **how many standard errors away from the hypothesised value** your sample mean is.
- T-values are useful because they are **standardised** measures of difference (like a z-score).

You don't need to know how to calculate a t-value yourself!

R will **translate our observed sample mean into a t-value** and **compare** it to this t-distribution for us.

But the way we compare t-values to this null distribution is basically the same as you've seen in previous weeks.

# Step 3: Calculate the test statistic for our observed sample

## We'll let R calculate our sample's t-statistic

<br>

We'll use the function `t.test()` and give it four arguments:

```{r include=F}
options(digits = 5)
ttest <- t.test(
  temp_sample$BodyTemp,       # which column of which dataframe do we want to test?
  mu = 37,                    # what value do we want to compare it to?
  alternative = 'two.sided',  # is our H1 'two.sided', 'greater', or 'less'?
  conf.level = .95            # 1 minus our significance level of .05
)
```


```{r eval=F}
t.test(
  temp_sample$BodyTemp,       # which column of which dataframe do we want to test?
  mu = 37,                    # what value do we want to compare it to?
  alternative = 'two.sided',  # is our H1 'two.sided', 'greater', or 'less'?
  conf.level = .95            # 1 minus our significance level of .05
)
```


## We'll let R calculate our sample's t-statistic {visibility='uncounted'}

<br>

We'll use the function `t.test()` and give it four arguments:

```{r}
t.test(
  temp_sample$BodyTemp,       # which column of which dataframe do we want to test?
  mu = 37,                    # what value do we want to compare it to?
  alternative = 'two.sided',  # is our H1 'two.sided', 'greater', or 'less'?
  conf.level = .95            # 1 minus our significance level of .05
)
```



## Let's break down this output (1)

<br>

```{r echo=F}
cat('', paste0(capture.output(
  ttest
), '\n')[4:5])
```

<br>

Our sample's t-value is –3.14 (that means it's three-and-a-bit SEs below the hypothesised population mean of 37).

The null distribution has 49 df (good sense check).

The p-value tells us that, if H0 were true, the probability of observing a t-value of –3 or more extreme, or +3 or more extreme, is .003, or 0.3%.

<br>
<br>

```{r echo=F, fig.width=8, fig.height=4, warning = F}
#| out.width: 1000px
tval <- -3.14
p_t49 +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -tval, colour = 'darkorchid', linewidth = 2, linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_vline(xintercept = tval, colour = 'darkorchid', linewidth = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      x = ifelse(x <= tval, x, NA),
      ymin = 0,  ymax = y),
    alpha = 0.5, fill = 'darkorchid'
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      x = ifelse(x >= -tval, x, NA),
      ymin = 0,  ymax = y),
    alpha = 0.5, fill = 'darkorchid'
  ) +
  NULL
```

## Let's break down this output (2)

<br>

```{r echo=F}
cat('', paste0(capture.output(
  ttest
), '\n')[6])
```

This line says in words what we wrote earlier as $\mu \neq 37$.

A non-directional alternative hypothesis, because the RQ didn't specify a difference in one direction or the other.

<br>

```{r echo=F}
cat('', paste0(capture.output(
  ttest
), '\n')[7:8])
```

This is the range of values within which we are 95% confident that the true population mean body temperature lies.
(Careful: **not** the range of values that, with 95% probability, contains that true value.)

<br>

```{r echo=F}
cat('', paste0(capture.output(
  ttest
), '\n')[9:11])
```

The mean body temperature observed in our sample is 36.8 degrees C.

This is the value that's three SEs below the hypothesised population mean of 37.


# Step 4: Make a decision about whether or not to reject H0

## Make a decision

```{r echo=F}
cat('', paste0(capture.output(
  ttest
), '\n'))
```

```{r echo=F, fig.width=10, fig.height=3, warning = F}
#| out.width: 1400px
p_t49 +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -tval, colour = 'darkorchid', linewidth = 2, linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_vline(xintercept = tval, colour = 'darkorchid', linewidth = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      x = ifelse(x <= tval, x, NA),
      ymin = 0,  ymax = y),
    alpha = 0.5, fill = 'darkorchid'
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      x = ifelse(x >= -tval, x, NA),
      ymin = 0,  ymax = y),
    alpha = 0.5, fill = 'darkorchid'
  ) +
  NULL
```

Our significance level, or alpha level, is .05 (or 5%).

Recall: When $\alpha = .05$, we accept that we will reject H0, even when H0 is true, one time in twenty.

**Our p-value .003 is below .05. This means our decision is to reject H0.**



# Step 5: Interpret decision in the context of RQ

## Interpret and report in the context of our RQ

<br>

**RQ: In healthy adults, is average body temperature different from the standard reference value of 37C?**

<br>

APA-formatted write-up:

> To investigate whether the mean body temperature of healthy humans (which we call $\mu$) differs from the commonly thought value of 37°C, we performed a one-sample t-test of $H_0 : \mu = 37$ against $H_1 : \mu \neq 37$ at the 5% significance level.
>
> The sample results (M = 36.81, SD = `r sd(temp_sample$BodyTemp) |> round(2)`) provided strong evidence against the null hypothesis ($t$(49) = –3, $p$ = .003, two-sided).
> We therefore conclude that the mean body temperature of healthy humans differs from 37°C and, with 95% confidence, is between 36.69°C and 36.93°C.

<br>

Note that this difference is statistically significant, but it's not practically significant: no one will rewrite the medical textbooks to change 37 to 36.81!

In Block 3, you'll learn a way to estimate how practically significant a difference might be.

<br>

## Distributions from warm-up Wooclap (1)

Uncollapse code for the basic standard normal distribution plot.

```{r fig.width=7, fig.align='center', fig.height = 4}
#| code-fold: true
dapr1blue <- '#0F4C81'

m <- 0
sd <- 1
nx <- seq(m-4*sd, m+4*sd, length.out = 1000)

p_stdnorm <- tibble(
  x = nx,
  n_dens = dnorm(nx, m = m, sd = sd)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = n_dens)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5, colour = dapr1blue) +
  labs(
    y = 'Density',
    x = 'Standard normal distribution'
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(family = 'Source Sans 3', size = 24),
    axis.title = ggplot2::element_text(color = dapr1blue)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(
    (m - 4*sd), (m + 4*sd), by = sd)
    ) +
  NULL
```

Uncollapse code for the following plot with the z-statistic and shaded area.

```{r fig.width=8, fig.align='center', fig.height = 4, warning = F}
#| code-fold: true
z <- 1.2
p_stdnorm +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      x = ifelse(x >= z, x, NA),
      ymin = 0,  ymax = n_dens),
    alpha = 0.3, fill = dapr1blue
    ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = z, colour = 'tomato1', linewidth = 2) +
  NULL
```
